body:
Why did national education become important?

National education formed a major part of the Swadeshi programme. Nationalists argued that education should help Indians develop knowledge, practical skills and confidence in their own society, rather than remain dependent on institutions controlled by the colonial government.

Discontent with government educational policies deepened during the anti-partition agitation. The Carlyle Circular of 1905, which sought to restrain students' political participation, intensified demands for educational alternatives.

The aim was not to reject modern learning. Supporters wanted institutions under Indian direction that could teach literature, science and technical subjects, while giving greater importance to Indian languages and national needs.

The National Council of Education, Bengal

The National Council of Education, Bengal was established on 11 March 1906 to organise education along national lines and under national control. It provided an institutional framework for the educational movement.

Satis Chandra Mukherjee, associated with the Dawn Society, played an important role in developing the idea of national education and helping organise the council's educational programme.

The Bengal National College and School was inaugurated on 14 August 1906, and classes began on 15 August 1906. Aurobindo Ghose was the first principal of Bengal National College.

The council and the college should not be treated as the same institution. The council was the organisation responsible for promoting a wider educational system; the college was one of the institutions established through that initiative.

Aurobindo Ghose had earlier worked in the princely state of Baroda, in present-day Gujarat, including teaching at Baroda College. He later became closely involved in Bengal's nationalist politics and national education.

Songs, literature and symbols

Swadeshi was also supported by songs, literature and images that helped communicate ideas of national unity and sacrifice. These were important because a public movement needed forms of expression that people could recognise beyond formal political speeches.

Vande Mataram

Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote Vande Mataram in the 1870s. It was later included in his novel Anandamath and became widely sung during the Swadeshi agitation.

The song expressed devotion to the motherland and became a recognisable nationalist symbol. Its composition preceded the 1905 movement; it was not written for the first time during the partition protests.

Abanindranath Tagore and Bharat Mata

In 1905, Abanindranath Tagore painted a well-known image of Bharat Mata. The figure represented the nation in symbolic form and was associated with ideas of learning, sustenance and service.

Rabindranath Tagore contributed to the cultural expression of the anti-partition movement through songs and the promotion of symbolic unity, including the tying of rakhi on the day the partition came into effect.

Distinguish the contributors

  • Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay: composed Vande Mataram.
  • Abanindranath Tagore: painted the well-known Bharat Mata image in 1905.
  • Rabindranath Tagore: supported anti-partition unity through cultural activity and the rakhi observance.
  • Aurobindo Ghose: first principal of Bengal National College.

What did national education contribute?

National education gave swadeshi a constructive dimension. Instead of relying only on protest against colonial policies, supporters sought to build Indian institutions capable of teaching useful knowledge and developing skills. It linked the demand for self-government with the idea that Indians should organise and manage important parts of their social and economic life.

Prelims focus

  • National Council of Education, Bengal: established on 11 March 1906.
  • Bengal National College and School: inaugurated on 14 August 1906; classes began on 15 August 1906.
  • First principal of Bengal National College: Aurobindo Ghose.
  • Vande Mataram: composed by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and included in Anandamath.
  • Bharat Mata painting of 1905: Abanindranath Tagore.
  • Trap: The National Council of Education and Bengal National College were different institutions.

[National Council of Education, Bengal, Golden Foundation, account of the council's establishment and the college's inauguration, consulted 21 November 2026; National Council of Education, Bengal, Transition NCEB, sections on curriculum and commencement of classes, consulted 21 November 2026; Sri Aurobindo Institute, Bengal National College: Sri Aurobindo (1906–1910), institutional history, consulted 21 November 2026; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World – II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, section 4, printed pp. 70–72; NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, chapter 9, printed pp. 113–114.]

pictures.caption: National education sought to bring learning under Indian direction during the Swadeshi era.

title: National Education and Cultural Symbols of the Swadeshi Movement

body:
The regional leaders of assertive nationalism

Assertive nationalist politics developed in several regions rather than emerging from a single provincial organisation. The phrase Lal–Bal–Pal brings together 3 prominent leaders who opposed excessive reliance on petitions and encouraged Indians to pursue self-government through stronger political action.

LeaderRegionPrincipal association
Lala Lajpat RaiPunjabAssertive nationalism and wider public mobilisation.
Bal Gangadhar TilakMaharashtraSwaraj, self-reliance and criticism of colonial rule through Kesari.
Bipin Chandra PalBengalPromotion of assertive nationalism and the Swadeshi Movement.

These regional associations are useful for identification questions. They should not be interpreted as restricting each leader's influence to a single province. Their political ideas circulated nationally.

Why was the Calcutta session of 1906 significant?

During the anti-partition movement, the Indian National Congress faced growing disagreement over how strongly it should challenge British rule. The annual Congress session held at Calcutta in December 1906 attempted to accommodate both Moderate and Extremist positions.

Dadabhai Naoroji, a respected senior nationalist, presided over this session. His leadership helped maintain an organisational compromise despite the differences between the 2 tendencies.

The important resolutions

The Calcutta session supported the reversal of Bengal's partition and adopted positions associated with the developing nationalist programme. Its decisions are commonly remembered through 4 connected ideas:

  • Swaraj: The demand for self-government became an explicit Congress objective.
  • Swadeshi: The Congress supported the use and development of Indian products and enterprises.
  • Boycott: The session upheld the boycott movement in Bengal, where extraordinary circumstances had arisen from the partition.
  • National education: The Congress supported education organised on national lines and criticised colonial educational policy.

These resolutions combined political aspiration with practical methods. Swaraj described the desired direction of political change; boycott and swadeshi applied economic pressure and promoted Indian enterprise; national education sought to build institutions under Indian direction.

What did swaraj mean at this stage?

In the context of the 1906 Congress session, the demand for swaraj was expressed as self-government, with the status enjoyed by self-governing parts of the British Empire serving as a reference point. It should not automatically be treated as identical to the later formal demand for complete independence.

This distinction is important because political terms can acquire more extensive meanings as a movement develops. A question about the 1906 session should be answered according to the position adopted at that time, not by transferring a later objective backward into history.

Why did the compromise remain unstable?

The 1906 resolutions did not settle how far the boycott should extend or how confrontational Congress methods should become. Extremist leaders wanted the adopted programme pursued firmly, while many Moderates remained concerned about a broad boycott of colonial institutions and about the consequences of confrontation.

These unresolved differences became central to the dispute at the Surat session of 1907.

Prelims focus

  • Calcutta Congress session: December 1906.
  • President of the 1906 session: Dadabhai Naoroji.
  • Important ideas: swaraj, swadeshi, boycott and national education.
  • The Congress supported the anti-partition movement and upheld boycott in Bengal.
  • Lal–Bal–Pal: Punjab, Maharashtra and Bengal respectively.
  • Trap: The 1906 demand for self-government should not be described without qualification as the later formal demand for complete independence.

[Indian National Congress, Synopsis of Plenary Sessions from 1885 to 2018, entry Twenty-Second Session, Calcutta, 1906, published 1 February 2023, consulted 21 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, chapter 9, printed pp. 112–114; Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, To the Gates of Freedom, account of the Twenty-Second Congress Session, Calcutta, 1906, consulted 21 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The 1906 Calcutta Congress linked swaraj with swadeshi, boycott and national education, and sought reversal of Bengal partition.
pictures.caption: The 1906 Calcutta session brought 4 connected nationalist ideas into the Congress programme.

title: Lal–Bal–Pal and the Calcutta Congress Session of 1906

body:
The background to the split

The Surat Split of 1907 was an organisational division within the Indian National Congress between its Moderate and Extremist tendencies. It occurred during the Congress session held at Surat in December 1907.

The immediate background was the uneasy compromise reached at Calcutta in 1906. The Congress had supported swaraj, swadeshi, boycott and national education, but its leaders disagreed about the interpretation and practical extent of these policies.

The central disagreements

Moderate leaders preferred constitutional agitation and were reluctant to extend boycott broadly to British institutions. They feared that such methods could encourage coercion and make organised political work more difficult.

Extremist leaders argued that the Congress should retain a strong commitment to the Calcutta programme and use effective public pressure rather than depend mainly on petitions.

The dispute therefore concerned both the methods of political struggle and control over the Congress organisation.

Why was the session held at Surat?

The 1907 Congress session had originally been proposed for Nagpur. Disagreement over the likely influence of Extremist leaders, including proposals connected with Tilak's leadership, contributed to moving the venue to Surat.

Surat is in present-day Gujarat. This gives the episode a direct geographical connection with Gujarat's place in the history of the national movement.

The presidential dispute

Moderate leaders supported Rash Behari Ghosh as the president for the Surat session. Leaders of the Extremist tendency opposed this arrangement, and some wanted Lala Lajpat Rai to preside. Lajpat Rai did not agree to take the position under the circumstances.

The proposed programme of the session also intensified the disagreement. Extremist leaders feared that the commitments to swaraj, swadeshi, boycott and national education adopted at Calcutta would be weakened or set aside.

What happened during the session?

Disagreement over the presidency and the agenda led to disorder at the Congress gathering. Proceedings broke down amid disturbances, and the session was suspended.

The result was a split between the Moderate and Extremist wings of the Congress. The incident is commonly called the Surat Split.

A suspended session is not a completed policy settlement

Rash Behari Ghosh is listed as president in Congress accounts of the suspended Surat session. The proceedings, however, broke down. The meeting should not be described as having successfully completed an agreed programme of resolutions.

Consequences for the Congress

After the split, the Moderates remained in control of the Congress organisation, while Tilak's followers and other Extremist leaders largely operated outside its formal structure. The division weakened immediate organisational unity at a time when the anti-partition movement had encouraged stronger public action.

The division was not permanent. The 2 tendencies were brought back together within the Congress in December 1915. This reconciliation restored a broader organisational basis for nationalist politics.

Surat Split and Bengal partition are different events

The partition of Bengal was a decision taken by the British government in 1905 to reorganise a province. The Surat Split was a division within the Indian National Congress in 1907. One involved colonial administration; the other involved disagreements among nationalist leaders.

Prelims focus

  • Surat Split: December 1907.
  • Original proposed venue for the 1907 session: Nagpur.
  • Moderate presidential choice at Surat: Rash Behari Ghosh.
  • Important Extremist leaders in the dispute included Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Lala Lajpat Rai.
  • Reunion of the Moderate and Extremist tendencies within Congress: December 1915.
  • Trap: Surat 1907 was a split within Congress, not the partition of Bengal or a division of Indian territory.

[Indian National Congress, Synopsis of Plenary Sessions from 1885 to 2018, entries Calcutta, 1906 and Suspended Session, Surat, 1907, published 1 February 2023, consulted 21 November 2026; Indian National Congress, INC Timeline, period 1905–1915, consulted 21 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, chapter 9, printed pp. 113–114.]

pictures.alt: Congress accepted the Calcutta programme in December 1906, split at Surat in December 1907, and reunited its two tendencies in December 1915.
pictures.caption: The Surat Split grew from unresolved differences after Calcutta and was followed by later reunion.

title: Surat Split of 1907: Causes, Events and Consequences
